get_model_param_grid <- function(df, modelType, numParams, randomSeed) {

    # mtry is finalized on the predictors only, so its upper bound is the number of predictors (excludes target and Id)
    dfPredictors <- df %>% select(-target, -Id)

    set.seed(randomSeed)
    param_spec <- switch(modelType,
                         glmnet = parameters(penalty(), mixture()),
                         kernlab = parameters(cost(), rbf_sigma(), svm_margin()),
                         # learn_rate is on a log10 scale. The dials default (1e-10 to 1e-1) spends most of the grid on rates
                         # so small that 1,000 trees barely move from the starting prediction: those fits take the full time
                         # and are never competitive. 10^-2.5 to 10^-0.5 (~0.003 to ~0.3) covers the useful range; the best
                         # rate found with the default range was ~0.07, comfortably inside it.
                         xgboost = parameters(min_n(), tree_depth(), learn_rate(range = c(-2.5, -0.5))),
                         ranger = parameters(min_n(), finalize(mtry(), dfPredictors)))

    dfParamGrid <- grid_space_filling(param_spec, size = numParams, type = "max_entropy")
    return(dfParamGrid)
}


# Workflow for a model
########################################################################################################################################################
# The data is already preprocessed, so the workflow only names the outcome and predictors.
# Id is excluded from the predictors: it is a row identifier, and with training Ids 1-1460 and test Ids 1461-2919,
# tree models would otherwise split on it and treat every test property as lying beyond the training range.
get_workflow <- function(model_spec) {
    workflow() %>%
        add_variables(outcomes = target, predictors = -Id) %>%
        add_model(model_spec)
}


# Cross Validation Results
########################################################################################################################################################
# tune_grid() fits every grid point on every fold. With parallel_over = "everything", each (fold, grid point)
# combination is a separate task, so all workers stay busy until the end of the run.
# The mean RMSE across folds is the same metric as before (mean of the per-fold RMSE).
cross_validate_model <- function(cv_folds, model_spec, param_grid) {

    tune_results <- get_workflow(model_spec) %>%
        tune_grid(resamples = cv_folds,
                  grid = param_grid,
                  metrics = metric_set(rmse),
                  control = control_grid(parallel_over = "everything"))

    dfResults <- tune_results %>%
        collect_metrics() %>%
        select(all_of(names(param_grid)), mean_rmse = mean) %>%
        arrange(mean_rmse)
    return(dfResults)
}


# Fitted model with parameters
########################################################################################################################################################
# Returns a fitted workflow; predict() on it selects the predictor columns from new data, so Id can stay in the data.
# The seed makes the final ranger and xgboost fits reproducible between runs.
get_fitted_model <- function(df, model_spec, dfParams, randomSeed = 2300) {

    model_wf <- get_workflow(model_spec)
    if(!is.null(dfParams)) model_wf <- model_wf %>% finalize_workflow(dfParams)
    set.seed(randomSeed)
    fit(model_wf, data = df)
}


# Parallel backend
########################################################################################################################################################
# Each worker is a separate R session with tidymodels and the model packages loaded. In a full run with 5 workers,
# no R process exceeded 0.6 GB and all R processes together (main session + workers) peaked at 3.2 GB. Budgeting
# 0.75 GB per worker leaves headroom. Workers are capped at cores - 1 (to keep the machine responsive) and at what fits in 70% of the RAM
# available when the run starts, so the run cannot push the machine into swapping even if other applications are open.
gb_per_worker <- 0.75
gb_available <- ps::ps_system_memory()$avail / 1024^3
num_workers <- max(1, min(parallel::detectCores() - 1, floor(0.7 * gb_available / gb_per_worker)))
message(sprintf("Using %d parallel workers (%.1f GB RAM available)", num_workers, gb_available))
plan(multisession, workers = num_workers)

# Create cross validation folds
cv_folds <- get_cv_folds(dfTrain_Proc, numFolds = 5, strataVar = "target", randomSeed = 2300, shuffleData = T)

# Compare the encodings of ordered factors with a linear model on the same folds (reported in the post)
compare_encoding <- function(ordinalScores) {

    df <- get_preprocessing_recipe(dfTrain, ordinalScores) %>%
        bake(new_data = NULL) %>%
        rename(target = SalePrice) %>%
        select(target, everything())
    folds <- get_cv_folds(df, numFolds = 5, strataVar = "target", randomSeed = 2300, shuffleData = T)
    vAliased <- map_int(folds$splits, ~ sum(is.na(coef(lm(target ~ ., data = analysis(.x) %>% select(-Id))))))

    tibble(encoding = if(ordinalScores) "ordinal scores" else "polynomial contrasts",
           predictors = ncol(df) - 2,
           folds_rank_deficient = sum(vAliased > 0),
           lm_cv_rmse = suppressWarnings(get_workflow(get_model_spec("lm")) %>%
                                             fit_resamples(resamples = folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) %>%
                                             collect_metrics() %>%
                                             pull(mean)))
}
dfEncodingComparison <- bind_rows(compare_encoding(ordinalScores = FALSE), compare_encoding(ordinalScores = TRUE))

# Time each model so the post can report relative run times
dfTimings <- tibble(model = character(), seconds = numeric())
time_model <- function(model, expr) {
    t0 <- Sys.time()
    result <- force(expr)
    dfTimings <<- dfTimings %>% add_row(model = model, seconds = as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs")))
    result
}

# lm model (no hyperparameters, so fit_resamples instead of tune_grid)
model_spec_lm <- get_model_spec(modelType = "lm")
cv_results_lm <- time_model("lm",
    get_workflow(model_spec_lm) %>%
        fit_resamples(resamples = cv_folds, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) %>%
        collect_metrics() %>%
        select(mean_rmse = mean))

# glmnet model
model_spec_glmnet <- get_model_spec(modelType = "glmnet")
param_grid_glmnet <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "glmnet", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)
cv_results_glmnet <- time_model("glmnet", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_glmnet, param_grid_glmnet))
param_best_glmnet <- cv_results_glmnet %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)
model_final_glmnet <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_glmnet, param_best_glmnet)

# kernlab model
model_spec_kernlab <- get_model_spec(modelType = "kernlab")
param_grid_kernlab <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "kernlab", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)
cv_results_kernlab <- time_model("kernlab", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_kernlab, param_grid_kernlab))
param_best_kernlab <- cv_results_kernlab %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)
model_final_kernlab <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_kernlab, param_best_kernlab)

# random forest model (ranger engine; objects keep the _rf names used in index.Rmd)
model_spec_rf <- get_model_spec(modelType = "ranger")
param_grid_rf <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "ranger", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)
cv_results_rf <- time_model("ranger", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_rf, param_grid_rf))
param_best_rf <- cv_results_rf %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)
model_final_rf <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_rf, param_best_rf)

# xgboost model
model_spec_xgboost <- get_model_spec(modelType = "xgboost")
param_grid_xgboost <- get_model_param_grid(dfTrain_Proc, modelType = "xgboost", numParams = 25, randomSeed = 2300)
cv_results_xgboost <- time_model("xgboost", cross_validate_model(cv_folds, model_spec_xgboost, param_grid_xgboost))
param_best_xgboost <- cv_results_xgboost %>% slice(1) %>% select(-mean_rmse)
model_final_xgboost <- get_fitted_model(dfTrain_Proc, model_spec_xgboost, param_best_xgboost)

plan(sequential)

# the results that the post uses, which are saved to Ames_Tuning.Rda
vTuningResults <- c("model_spec_lm", "model_spec_glmnet", "model_spec_rf", "model_spec_xgboost", "model_spec_kernlab",
                    "model_final_glmnet", "model_final_rf", "model_final_xgboost", "model_final_kernlab", "cv_results_lm",
                    "cv_results_glmnet", "cv_results_rf", "cv_results_xgboost", "cv_results_kernlab", "param_grid_glmnet",
                    "param_grid_rf", "param_grid_xgboost", "param_grid_kernlab", "param_best_glmnet", "param_best_rf",
                    "param_best_xgboost", "param_best_kernlab", "dfTrain", "dfTest", "dfTrain_Proc",
                    "dfTest_Proc", "dfTimings", "get_preprocessing_recipe", "preprocessing_recipe", "vFeaturesCollinear",
                    "dfEncodingComparison", "cv_folds", "vFeaturesSkew")

And this code decides whether to load the saved results or to run the tuning steps:

# The clean dataset from Part 1
ames_data_file <- "../ames-housing-part1-data-pipeline/Ames_Housing_Clean.Rda"

# Fingerprint (hash) of the inputs of the tuning: the data that it uses, and the code of the "tuning_steps"
# chunk, which also sets the hyperparameter grids. Comments and spacing are removed from the code first, so
# editing them does not start a new tuning run.
envData <- new.env()
load(ames_data_file, envir = envData)
tuning_steps <- knitr::knit_code$get("tuning_steps")
tuning_hash <- rlang::hash(list(data = list(envData$dfClean, envData$vTestIDs),
                                code = deparse(parse(text = tuning_steps, keep.source = FALSE))))

# If the saved results were made from the same inputs, load them. Otherwise, tune the models again and save
# the new results together with the fingerprint of their inputs.
envSaved <- new.env()
if (file.exists("Ames_Tuning.Rda")) load("Ames_Tuning.Rda", envir = envSaved)
if (identical(envSaved$tuning_hash, tuning_hash)) {
  list2env(as.list(envSaved), envir = environment())
} else {
  eval(parse(text = tuning_steps))
  save(list = c(vTuningResults, "tuning_hash"), file = "Ames_Tuning.Rda")
}
rm(envData, envSaved)

item.title: Ames Housing - Part 2 - Walkthrough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Ames Housing - Part 1 - Laying the foundation - Building a Data Pipeline
  • Ames Housing - Part 3 - Closing the deal - Building Models

In Part 1, we built a data pipeline that cleans the Ames Housing dataset and creates new features. In this post, we explore the finalized dataset. An exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first study of a dataset before we build models. We look at the features one at a time, then two and three at a time, to find which features affect the sale price. In Part 3, we use what we learn to build models.

Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a Time

In this section, we look at each feature by itself.

Numerical Features

First, let’s plot all the features that measure an area in square feet:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, vFeaturesNum[str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")])

What’s notable?

  • All the area features have outliers, which are values that are very different from most other values.
  • Many features are very skewed: most values are small and a few values are much larger. Before we build models, we must transform these features (for example, with a log) to make them less skewed.

Now let’s look at the other numerical features:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, setdiff(vFeaturesNum[!str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")], "SalePrice"))

What’s notable?

  • Most properties were sold less than 20 years after they were built or remodeled.

Let’s plot SalePrice on a log scale. On a log scale, each step on the axis multiplies the value by the same amount:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, "SalePrice", nBins = 50, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

What’s notable?

  • The distribution has long tails on both sides: a few properties are much cheaper or much more expensive than most.
  • 11 properties cost less than USD 50,000, and 17 properties cost more than USD 500,000.
  • Outliers have a strong effect on linear models.

Categorical Features

Ordinal Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat1, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In many features, 1 or 2 categories are much more common than the others. This makes these features hard to use for predictions, because the data has only a few examples of the other categories.

Nominal Features.

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat2, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In many features, 1 or 2 categories are much more common than the others.
  • Most properties are sold in the summer months, and the fewest in the winter months.
  • The data shows the effect of the housing market crisis: the fewest properties were sold in 2010.

Bivariate Analysis: Two Features at a Time

Numerical-Numerical

Let’s look at how SalePrice changes with each of the other numerical features. A scatter plot shows one dot for each property, and the line shows the best straight line through the dots (a regression line):

eda_plot_scatter(dfClean, vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)

Let’s look more closely at TotalSF. The labels show the properties with the largest Cook’s distance. Cook’s distance measures how much one point pulls the regression line towards itself:

eda_plot_scatter(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "Id", labelBy = "cooks")

# Cook's distance of each property in a linear fit of SalePrice on TotalSF
dfInfluence <- dfClean %>% select(Id, TotalSF, SalePrice) %>% drop_na()
dfInfluence <- dfInfluence %>%
  mutate(cooks = cooks.distance(lm(SalePrice ~ TotalSF, data = dfInfluence))) %>%
  arrange(desc(cooks))

vOutliers_TotalSF <- dfInfluence$Id[1:3]

What’s notable?

  • The scatter plot of TotalSF and SalePrice clearly shows a few very large properties that sold at unusually low prices. These points have high leverage: they are far from the other points, so they pull the regression line strongly. Without them, the line would be steeper.
  • The same properties also affect TotalBsmtSF.
  • The Ids of these properties are 1299,2550,524. Their Cook’s distances are 5.69, 2.46, 0.54. These values are much higher than the usual limit of 4/n = 0.0014, where n is the number of properties. The next property has a Cook’s distance of only 0.12. Of these three properties, 524 and 1299 are in the training set.

Transforming Skewed Features

Many numerical features are right skewed. Can we change them with a simple formula (a transform), so that their relationship with log(SalePrice) becomes closer to a straight line? Let’s compare common transforms of three features: TotalSF, the strongest area feature; LotArea, which is very skewed; and GarageArea, which is almost not skewed. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points. R-squared is a number from 0 to 1. It tells how much of the variation in log(SalePrice) the line explains:

lTransformPlots <- map(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"), ~ eda_plot_transforms(dfClean, .x, "SalePrice"))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lTransformPlots, ncol = 1)

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2 <- map(lTransformPlots, ~ .x$data %>%
             distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
             pull(r_squared) %>%
             set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))) %>%
  set_names(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"))
r2 <- function(feature, transform) round(vR2[[feature]][transform], 3)

# skewness of each feature
vSkew <- map_dbl(c(TotalSF = "TotalSF", LotArea = "LotArea", GarageArea = "GarageArea"), ~ timeDate::skewness(dfClean[[.x]], na.rm = T))

What’s notable?

  • A log transform almost doubles the R-squared of LotArea (skewness 12.8), from 0.066 to 0.138. Without the transform, a few very large lots control the line. The log makes these large values smaller.
  • All the transforms improve TotalSF (skewness 1.5) a little. With a log, the R-squared goes from 0.61 to 0.647.
  • GarageArea (skewness 0.2) is almost not skewed, and the transforms make the fit worse. With a log, the R-squared goes down from 0.426 to 0.389. Also, the log cannot use the properties without a garage, because the log of 0 does not exist.
  • So, before we build linear models, we should transform only the very skewed features, not all of them.

Correlations with SalePrice

We keep the features whose correlation with SalePrice is at least 0.1 or at most -0.1. The Pearson correlation measures how close a relationship is to a straight line, so outliers and skewed features affect it strongly. The Spearman correlation uses the ranks of the values (1st, 2nd, 3rd, …) instead of the values. So it measures whether one feature always goes up (or always goes down) when the other goes up, even along a curve. If we compare the two, we can see which relationships are strong but not straight lines:

library(corrr)

dfCor <- dfClean[vFeaturesNum] %>% 
  correlate() %>% 
  focus(SalePrice) %>% 
  dplyr::rename(feature = term,
                corr = SalePrice) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(corr))) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(abs(corr) > 0.1) %>% 
  mutate(corr = round(corr, 2)) %>% 
  mutate(feature = fct_reorder(feature, corr)) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(!(feature %in% vFeatures_to_exclude))

vFeaturesCor <- dfCor %>% pull(feature) %>% as.character()

p1 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "pearson", minAbsCor = 0.1)
p2 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "spearman", minAbsCor = 0.1)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 2)

# compare Pearson and Spearman correlations
dfCorMethods <- tibble(feature = setdiff(vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice")) %>%
  mutate(pearson = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")),
         spearman = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")))
cor_of <- function(feature_name, method) round(dfCorMethods[[method]][dfCorMethods$feature == feature_name], 2)

What’s notable?

  • The 5 most correlated features are TotalSF, GarageArea, TotalBath, TotalBsmtSF, 1stFlrSF. A buyer would naturally look at these features to judge a property and its price.
  • PropertyAge has a strong negative correlation with SalePrice. This means that newer properties sell for higher prices than older properties.
  • For most features, the Pearson and Spearman correlations are similar. But LotArea is different: its correlation goes up from 0.27 to 0.43. Larger lots do sell for more, but the relationship is far from a straight line. The log transform above partly corrects this.
  • For BsmtFinSF1, the correlation goes down from 0.43 to 0.33. About 32% of the properties have no finished basement, so they all have the same rank. Also, the largest finished basements have a large effect on the Pearson correlation. So the straight-line relationship with SalePrice seems stronger than the rank relationship.

Numerical-Categorical (Ordinal)

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat1,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In almost all of these features, SalePrice clearly changes with the order of the categories.
  • The overall quality and the exterior quality show some of the strongest trends.

Numerical-Categorical (Nominal)

Now let’s look at SalePrice for the nominal features. The categories of a nominal feature have no natural order. But if we sort the categories by their median SalePrice, we can find trends. To show the trends better, the SalePrice axis does not show the outliers. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat2,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • GarageType: buyers prefer built-in and attached garages to detached garages and other types.
  • The categories of MSSubClass show that houses built in 1946 or later have higher prices than older houses.

Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a Time

In this section, we look at how some related features change SalePrice together.

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

TotalSF and GarageArea have some of the strongest correlations with SalePrice. Let’s see how these relationships change with NeighborhoodType and GarageType:

p1 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", "NeighborhoodType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
p2 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "GarageArea", "SalePrice", "GarageType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

  • For the same total area, properties in some neighborhoods sell for more than in others.
  • The properties without a garage form a separate group.
  • For the same GarageArea, properties with built-in or attached garages usually sell for more.
  • So NeighborhoodType and GarageType explain some of the differences in SalePrice.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

The dots in the scatter plots overlap a lot. So let’s check these results in another way, and compare categories among properties of similar size. We split TotalSF and GarageArea into four groups (bins) with the same number of properties. Then we plot SalePrice for each category in each group. We also check whether central air conditioning (CentralAir) changes the price of properties of the same size:

p1 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p2 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "GarageType", "SalePrice", "GarageArea", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p3 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "CentralAir", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

# median SalePrice by category within each bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), category = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
lBinMedians <- map(list(neighborhood = p1, garage = p2, air = p3), get_bin_medians)
bin_median <- function(plotName, binNum, categoryName) {
  dfMedians <- lBinMedians[[plotName]]
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$category == categoryName], accuracy = 1)
}

What’s notable?

  • The neighborhood is very important, even for properties of the same size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice goes from $161,000 in Type5 neighborhoods to $327,000 in Type1 neighborhoods. Type1 neighborhoods have few or no properties in the smallest group, so the neighborhood and the size are also related.
  • For the same GarageArea, built-in and attached garages go with higher prices than detached garages. For the largest garages, the median SalePrice is $299,018 for built-in garages, $253,000 for attached garages and $140,000 for detached garages. Some garage types have very few properties, so their box plots are less reliable.
  • Properties with central air conditioning sell for more, at every size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice is $262,140 with central air and $136,000 without it.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

Does a combination of two categorical features tell us more about SalePrice? A heatmap answers this question. It is a grid of tiles, one tile for each combination of two categories:

p1 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "OverallQual", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p2 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "GarageType", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p3 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "MSSubClass", "MSZoning", "SalePrice")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

# number of combinations, and those with fewer than 10 properties
vCells <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ nrow(.x$data))
vSparse <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ sum(.x$data$n < 10))

Each tile shows the median SalePrice (by its color) and the number of properties. A tile is grey if it has fewer than 10 properties, because a median of so few properties is not reliable.

  • Some neighborhoods have more properties with a high OverallQual, so their prices are higher. But in Type4 neighborhoods, SalePrice clearly changes with the quality of the property.
  • It is less clear whether GarageType has a large effect by itself. Buyers seem to prefer built-in and attached garages, but NeighborhoodType explains most of the differences.
  • In both one-story and multi-story houses built after 1946, properties in low-density residential zones and floating village zones usually have higher prices.
  • Many combinations are rare: 11 of the 34 combinations of OverallQual and NeighborhoodType, and 20 of the 46 combinations of MSSubClass and MSZoning, have fewer than 10 properties. So we can compare only the common combinations reliably. Also, a model would find it hard to learn how these features work together.

Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
  • Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models

In the previous posts, we found out which attributes of a diamond are important for its price. An exploratory data analysis showed that carat, clarity and color are the most important features to predict price. Then we built linear models to predict the prices, and we chose the best model by its metrics.

In this post, we use non-linear models to predict the prices of diamonds, and we compare them with the linear models. A non-linear model can learn curved relationships and interactions between features by itself.

Training Non-linear Models

We use three types of non-linear models:

  • randomForest builds many decision trees and takes the average of their predictions. A decision tree predicts a value by asking a series of yes/no questions about the features, such as “Is carat more than 1?”.
  • xgboost (gradient boosting) builds many small decision trees one after the other. Each new tree corrects some of the errors of the trees before it.
  • keras builds a neural network. A neural network passes the features through layers of simple calculations, and it learns the strength of each connection from the data.

We follow some of the same steps as for the linear models, and we change some features:

  • Split the dataset into a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%.
  • Keep the same mix of clarity grades in both sets (stratified sampling).
  • clarity, color and cut have ordered categories, from the lowest grade to the highest grade. randomForest can use these categories directly. But xgboost and keras need all the features as numbers. There are two methods to change categories into numbers:
    1. One-hot encoding: each category of clarity, color and cut becomes a new feature with the values 0 and 1. A disadvantage of this method is that the order of the grades is lost. But the training set is large, so the non-linear models can learn the order by themselves.
    2. Integer scores: the grades become the numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, from the lowest grade to the highest. But this method assumes that the steps between all the grades are equal, which may not be correct here.
  • Center and scale all the values in the training set, so that all the features have similar ranges. Then put the features in a matrix (a table of numbers).
  • Train a non-linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls the random split into the training set and the testing set.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

Here are the average metrics for all the models that we trained with keras, randomForest and xgboost:

load("fit_models_keras.Rda")

dfModels_keras <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "keras")
best_model_results_keras <- best_model_results
dfResults_keras <- best_model_results_keras$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "keras")

load("fit_models_rf.Rda")

dfModels_rf <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")
best_model_results_rf <- best_model_results
dfResults_rf <- best_model_results_rf$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")

load("fit_models_xgb.Rda")

dfModels_xgb <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")
best_model_results_xgb <- best_model_results
dfResults_xgb <- best_model_results_xgb$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")

# combine the actual v/s predicted results from the best model using the 3 methods
dfResults <- map_df(list(dfResults_keras, dfResults_rf, dfResults_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  group_by(type)

# combine the average metrics from all the models using the 3 methods
dfModels <- map_df(list(dfModels_keras, dfModels_rf, dfModels_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  gather(avg_metric, value, rmse, rsq, mae)

# create an HTML table
dfModels %>% tidyHtmlTable(header = "type", cgroup1 = "avg_metric", cell_value = "value", rnames = "model", align = "|rrr|rrr|rrr")
keras randomForest xgboost
price ~ . c(“989.71”, “0.93”, “360.55”) c(“529.28”, “0.98”, “262.35”) c(“540.76”, “0.98”, “280.49”)

The R-squared values (rsq) show that all the models learn the complex relationship between price and carat very well. For the linear models, we had to change both price and carat to a log scale. The neural network and the decision tree models learn this relationship by themselves. The root mean squared error (RMSE) is in dollars, so it is easy to understand. The average price of a diamond is about $4000, and the prices vary by about $4000 (the standard deviation). So the RMSE values of the models are very low. With carat, clarity and color, the RMSE is between $572 and $645. The best linear model with the same features has an RMSE of about $816.

The exploratory data analysis helps here, because the models with only carat, clarity and color give excellent results. If we add cut, the RMSE goes down only a little.

Even the base models with all the features (price ~ .) explain the variation in the prices very well, although some of their features repeat the same information. Decision trees and neural networks are not affected by such repeated information (multicollinearity) as much as linear models are. To find the most important features of these models, we can explain their predictions one at a time.

Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations

LIME is a method to explain the predictions of a “black box” model, which is a model whose calculations are too complex for a person to follow. LIME explains one prediction at a time. It assumes that, close to a single diamond, the complex model behaves like a simple linear model. So LIME fits a simple model around that one diamond. The simple model then explains how the complex model makes its prediction for that diamond.

LIME uses these steps:

  • Take one diamond, and make many copies of it with small random changes to its features.
  • Measure how similar each copy is to the original diamond.
  • Use the complex model to predict the price of each copy.
  • Choose a small number (m) of features that best explain the predicted prices.
  • Fit a simple model to the copies, with the m features. Give more weight to the copies that are more similar to the original diamond.
  • Use the weights of the simple model to explain the prediction for the original diamond.

Here, we choose the 5 features that best explain the predictions for 6 random diamonds from the testing set.

# Plot Feature Importance by sample
plot_features(explanation_keras, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_features(explanation_xgb, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

For these 6 random diamonds, the most important features for the predictions are carat, clarity, color, x and y.

# Plot Feature Importance Heatmap
plot_explanations(explanation_keras) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_explanations(explanation_xgb) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

We know that x and y have a very strong correlation with carat, so they repeat the same information. That is why it is good practice to remove such repeated features before we train a model. For keras, the model with carat, clarity and color has the best metrics. For the decision tree models, the model with all the features is a little more accurate, but it needs many more features.

Actual v/s Predicted

Finally, here are the scatter plots of the actual prices against the predicted prices, for the best model of each type on the testing set:

p1 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(linear scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

p2 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(log scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

The scatter plots use both normal (linear) axes and log axes. The R-squared and RMSE values of the 3 methods are similar. But for expensive diamonds, the predictions of keras are more spread out than the predictions of the two decision tree methods. For cheap diamonds, the decision tree methods seem to predict the prices better, with less spread.

As with the linear models, the spread of the predicted prices increases with price. The decision tree methods keep their predictions close to the range of prices in the data. Their highest predictions are $18,340 (randomForest) and $19,118 (xgboost). The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,823. A randomForest prediction is an average of prices from the training data, so it cannot be higher than those prices. xgboost adds up many small corrections, so its predictions can be only a little higher. A neural network, like a linear model, can predict prices far above the prices in the data (extrapolation). The highest price that keras predicts is $26,591. So the non-linear methods learn the relationships between price and the other features very well, and the decision tree methods also keep their predictions within a reasonable range.

Summary

  • All 3 non-linear methods learn the complex relationship between price, carat and the other features by themselves. They do not need feature engineering.
  • The exploratory data analysis helps us remove repeated features before we train the models. This makes the training faster. For keras, it also gives much better metrics.
  • keras neural networks train the fastest, because they can use a GPU (a graphics processor that does many calculations at the same time).
  • Of the two decision tree methods, xgboost trains much faster than randomForest.
  • randomForest and xgboost can use several CPU cores at the same time. On a local computer, the amount of memory (RAM) is the only limit.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we explored the diamonds dataset. We found that price has a strong correlation with carat, x, y and z, and that log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also seemed to help predict the price.

In this post, we build linear models and find out how well they predict the price of diamonds. A linear model predicts a value by adding up the features, each multiplied by a number (a coefficient) that the model learns from the data.

The model summary shows that this model is overfitted. An overfitted model learns the noise in the data, not only the true patterns, so it does not work well on new data. For example, we know that depth and table have no effect on price, but the model says that they are very important.

The table above also shows the root mean squared error (RMSE) and other metrics. RMSE is the typical size of a prediction error, in the same units as the price. A lower RMSE means better predictions.

Let’s plot the actual prices against the predicted prices, to see how well this base model works.

  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted price from a base linear model")

If the predictions are good, the points are close to the dashed line at 45 degrees, where the predicted price is equal to the actual price. This base model predicts the prices badly. Worst of all, it predicts negative prices for cheap diamonds. To prevent such impossible results, we must use log(price) instead of price.

Feature Engineering

Feature engineering means that we create new features from the existing features, to make the patterns easier for a model to learn.

We know that the price of a diamond has a strong correlation with its size. If all other things are equal, a larger diamond has a higher price.

As a first estimate, we can treat a diamond as a box with the dimensions x, y and z. Then its volume is x * y * z. These 3 dimensions have a strong correlation with each other. So we can calculate one average dimension as the cube root of volume. This average dimension keeps a straight-line relationship with log(price).

We can also calculate an average dimension with high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related by this equation:

$ density = mass/volume $

1 carat is 0.2 grams. If we divide the mass by the density of diamond (3.51 grams per cubic centimeter), we get the volume. The cube root of the volume gives an average dimension.

dfInput <- diamonds %>%
  mutate(row = row_number(),
         volume = x*y*z,
         `average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),
         volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,
         `average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10)   # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mm

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "row", labelBy = "leverage") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")

# the point with the most leverage on the linear fit of price on the dimension-based feature
dfLeverage <- dfInput %>%
  mutate(leverage = hatvalues(lm(price ~ `average dimension`, data = dfInput))) %>%
  slice_max(leverage, n = 1)

The two methods give similar results, but the density method gives a narrower range. Which method is more reliable? In each panel, the labels show the row numbers of the diamonds with the most leverage. Leverage tells how much a point can pull the straight line towards itself. Points that are far from the others along the x axis have the most leverage. With the dimensions, the most extreme point is the diamond in row 24068. It is a 2 carat diamond with a recorded width y of 58.9 mm. This value is clearly a recording error. The other labelled points are diamonds with an average dimension of 0. Also, the density is a constant. So we do not need to divide by it to calculate the volume. Instead, we can take the cube root of carat itself. Then we expect a straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\). A straight-line relationship is what a linear model needs, because the model adds up its features in a straight-line way.

The geometry suggests a cube root. But does the cube root give the best straight line? Let’s compare it with other transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points of log(price):

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")

  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is much better than carat without a transform (0.847). But log(carat) is even better (0.933). A straight-line relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) is easy to understand: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price when carat increases by 1%. We will try both transforms in our models.

Training Linear Models

These are the steps to build the linear models and measure how well they work:

  • Split the dataset into two sets: a training set with 75% of the diamonds and a testing set with 25%. The model learns from the training set. Then we check its predictions on the testing set, which has diamonds that the model has not seen.
  • clarity is one of the most important features. So we split the data in a way that keeps the same mix of clarity grades in both sets. This is called stratified sampling.
  • Train (fit) a linear model on the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and calculate the metrics.
  • Put all the steps above in a function that takes the model formula and a random seed. The seed controls which diamonds go into each set. With different seeds, we get different random splits, so one lucky or unlucky split does not decide the results.
  • Run each model several times with different seeds, and calculate its average metrics. These averages show how well the model works on new data.

  select(price, everything()) %>% 
  initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")

dfTest <- testing(train_split)

We ran each model 5 times with different seeds. Here are the average metrics. R-squared (rsq) tells how much of the variation in price the model explains, and the mean absolute error (mae) is the average size of a prediction error:

fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {

  set.seed(randomSeed)
  train_split <- diamonds %>% 
    select(price, everything()) %>% 
    initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")
  
  dfTrain <- training(train_split)
  dfTest <- testing(train_split)

  # fit a linear model
  model_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)
  
  # predict on testing set to determine rmse  
  predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)

  # predict on testing set with outliers
  dfResults <- dfTest %>% 
    mutate(actual = price) %>% 
    mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% 
    select(actual, estimate)
  
  if(get_model) {
    return(list(model_lm, dfResults))
  } else {
    return(dfResults)
  }
}

Multiple R-squared:  0.982,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.982 
F-statistic: 1.53e+05 on 14 and 40438 DF,  p-value: <0.0000000000000002

A residual is the difference between the actual value and the predicted value, here of log(price). Residual plots show if the errors of a model have a pattern. If the model is good, the residuals look like random noise around 0. Here are the four standard residual plots of our final model:

# labels are off: the row numbers of a random training set do not identify the diamonds
eda_plot_residuals(fit_lm[[1]], nLabel = 0)

vStdResid <- rstandard(fit_lm[[1]])
vCooks <- cooks.distance(fit_lm[[1]])
  • Residuals vs Fitted: The residuals stay close to 0 for all predicted values, and the red smooth line is almost flat. So the model captures the relationship well. The small curve shows that a little non-linearity remains. At the highest predicted values, the residuals form a sloping edge below 0. The reason is that no diamond in the data costs more than $18,823, so for the largest predictions, the actual price can only be lower.
  • Normal Q-Q: In the middle, the points follow the dashed line, so most residuals are normally distributed. But the tails, especially the upper tail, are longer: some diamonds cost much more than the model predicts. 160 of the 40453 diamonds in the training set have a standardized residual larger than 3, or smaller than -3.
  • Scale-Location: The smooth line is almost flat, so the spread of the errors is about the same for cheap and expensive diamonds. The log of price makes the spread stable. Without it, the errors grow with the price.
  • Residuals vs Leverage: No diamond has a high leverage. The largest Cook’s distance is only 0.0067. A point needs a Cook’s distance of about 0.5 or more to pull the model strongly, so the plot does not even reach the dashed contours that mark 0.5 and 1. No single diamond controls the model.

If clarity and color do not change, a 1% increase in carat increases the predicted price by about 1.88%.

Here is a scatter plot of the actual prices against the prices that our final model predicts for the testing set:

fit_lm[[2]] %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = bquote(log(price) == log(carat) + clarity + color))

The points are close to the 45-degree line. But at the high end, the differences between the actual and predicted prices become larger. The predictions of the final model are also much less extreme. The most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,804. The highest predicted price is $28,130. But the cube root model predicts prices as high as $59,082 for the same testing set. Like all linear models, the final model can still predict prices above the highest prices in the data (this is called extrapolation).

item.title: Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
item.description:
In this case study, we explore the diamonds dataset. Then, in the next posts, we build models that predict the price of a diamond. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. Some models are linear (they use straight-line relationships) and some are non-linear (they can also learn curves).

Data Description

The diamonds dataset has almost 54,000 diamonds. For each diamond, it gives the price (in US dollars of 2008) and other attributes, such as the weight and the quality grades. We call each attribute a feature.

dfDescription <- tribble(~ Attribute, ~ Description,
                         "price", "price in 2008 USD",
                         "carat", "weight of a diamond (1 carat = 0.2 gms)",
                         "cut", "quality of the cut (Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal)",
                         "color", "diamond color from D (best) to J (worst)",
                         "clarity", "a measurement of how clear the diamond is (I1 (worst), SI2, SI1, VS2, VS1, VVS2, VVS1, IF (best))",
                         "x", "length in mm",
                         "y", "width in mm",
                         "z", "depth in mm",
                         "depth", "total depth percentage = z/mean(x, y)",
                         "table", "width of the top of diamond relative to widest point")

knitr::kable(dfDescription)

  • price: The average price of a diamond is about USD 4000. Many diamonds are much more expensive than most others. We call such unusual values outliers.
  • carat: The average weight is about 0.8 carat. About 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The 5 largest values show that there are many outliers at the high end.
  • cut: About 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut. Only 3% have a Fair cut. So the categories are not balanced: some categories have many more diamonds than others.
  • color: Most diamonds have a color grade from E to H. Fewer diamonds have the color grade J.
  • clarity: Most diamonds have a clarity grade from SI2 to VS1. About 1% have the worst grade, I1. Only about 3% have the best grade, IF.
  • depth: Most depth values are between 60 and 64. There are outliers at both the low end and the high end.
  • table: Most table values are between 54 and 65. There are outliers at both ends.
  • x: The length of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 4 and 8. Some values are 0, which means that nobody recorded them.
  • y: The width of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 3.5 and 8. 7 values are 0.
  • z: The depth of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 2.5 and 8.5. 20 values are 0.

Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a Time

In this section, we look at each feature by itself.

Numerical Features

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum)

The plots show outliers in each feature. Let’s remove the outliers and plot the features again. We use a common rule: a value is an outlier if it is more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median. The median is the middle value: half the values are below it and half are above it. The interquartile range is the width of the middle half of the values. The outliers themselves have almost no effect on these two numbers, so the rule is reliable. A rule that uses the average would be less reliable, because the outliers pull the average towards them.

makeOutliersNA <- function(Z) {
  # values more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median become NA
  ifelse(flag_outliers(Z, nIQR = 2.5), NA, Z)
}

# convert outliers to NA values
dfInput <- dfInput %>% mutate_at(vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA)

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum) + labs(title = "Histograms of numerical features excluding outliers")

Without the outliers, the ranges of the values are more reasonable. carat and price are right skewed: most values are small, and a few values are much larger.

Let’s plot price on a log scale. On a log scale, each step on the axis multiplies the value by the same amount (for example, from $100 to $1,000 to $10,000). This makes it easier to see the spread of skewed values:

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, "price", nBins = 100, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

The plot has two peaks. This means that two price ranges are the most common: one just below USD 1000 and one near USD 5000. Interestingly, almost no diamonds cost about USD 1500. So the plot shows a big gap at that price.

Categorical Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_column(dfInput, .x)), ncol = 2)

The plots clearly show that the categories of cut and clarity are not balanced.

Bivariate Analysis: Two Features at a Time

In this section, we look at how price changes with each of the other features.

Numerical-numerical

First, we measure the correlation of price with each numerical feature. A correlation is a number from -1 to 1. It tells how closely two features move together in a straight line. A value near 1 means that when one feature goes up, the other also goes up. A value near -1 means that the other goes down. A value near 0 means that there is no straight-line relationship.

eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfInput[vFeaturesNum] %>% drop_na(), outlineVar = "price", plotTitle = "Clustered correlations of numerical features")

price has a very strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. These four features are also strongly correlated with each other, because they all measure the size of a diamond. So a linear model cannot easily separate their effects. table and depth have almost no correlation with price. So they are not useful to predict the price.

Now let’s look at the scatter plots. A scatter plot shows one dot for each diamond:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

Without the outliers, price grows faster and faster as carat, x, y and z increase. So let’s plot price on a log scale:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLog = T, yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

On a log scale, log(price) has an approximately straight-line (linear) relationship with x, y and z. But its relationship with carat is still curved. Also, the spread (variance) of price increases as the diamonds get larger.

Can we change carat with a simple formula so that its relationship with log(price) becomes a straight line? We call such a change a transform. Let’s compare some common transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points. R-squared is a number from 0 to 1. It tells how much of the variation in log(price) the straight line explains. A higher value means that the line fits the points better:

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(dfInput, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

log(carat) gives the best straight-line fit, with an R-squared of 0.926. The cube root is second (0.919) and the square root is third (0.91). carat without a transform has the lowest R-squared, 0.862. So log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). This means that when the weight increases by a given percentage, the price increases by an approximately constant percentage. We will use this result when we create features for the models (Feature Engineering).

Numerical-Categorical

Let’s look at price for each category of the categorical features. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_box(dfInput, .x, "price", yLimits = c(300, 8000), 
                                                               yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))), ncol = 3)

To show the trends better, the price axis of these box plots does not show the most expensive diamonds. The box plots are surprising: for cut, color and clarity, the median price usually goes down as the grade gets better. This is very strange. We will find the reason in the multivariate analysis.

  • The median price goes down steadily from a Fair cut to an Ideal cut.
  • For color, the median price goes down from J (worst) to G (middle grade). Then it goes up, and it goes down again for D (best).
  • For clarity, the median price goes up from I1 to SI2. Then it goes down steadily to IF.

Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a Time

So far, we know that carat, x, y and z have the strongest relationship with price. The grades of cut, color and clarity also seem to have some effect on the median price. Let’s use scatter plots to look at these relationships together:

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, "carat", "price", .x, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), ncol = 2)

The dots overlap a lot. But for diamonds of the same carat weight, price clearly goes up as clarity gets better. color shows the same pattern, but it is weaker. cut does not show any effect.

So, for diamonds of the same weight, both color and clarity explain some of the differences in price.

All Features

Why do the diamonds with better grades seem cheaper in the bivariate analysis? To find out, we measure the association between every pair of features. An association tells how strongly two features are related. Here, we rank the grades of cut, color and clarity from worst to best. Then we can compare them with the numerical features with Spearman’s rank correlation. This correlation uses the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves, so it also works for grades:

eda_plot_association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T, outlineVar = "price",
                            plotTitle = "Spearman correlations, with grades ranked from worst to best")

mAssoc <- association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T)
  • carat has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.37) and with color (-0.24). This means that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.
  • price has a very strong correlation with carat (0.96). So price also has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.21) and with color (-0.13).
  • carat, x, y and z form a tight group, and they are almost perfectly correlated with each other. So, to predict the price, these features give almost the same information.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

In the scatter plots, the dots overlap too much to show how much each grade matters. So let’s compare grades among diamonds of similar weight. We split the diamonds into four groups (bins) of equal size by carat. Then we plot price for each grade in each group:

lBinPlots <- map(c("clarity", "color", "cut"), ~ eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfInput, .x, "price", "carat", yLog = T,
                                                                       yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lBinPlots, ncol = 1)

# median price by grade within each carat bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), grade = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
dfBinMedians_clarity <- get_bin_medians(lBinPlots[[1]])
bin_median <- function(dfMedians, binNum, gradeName) {
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$grade == gradeName], accuracy = 1)
}

# median carat by clarity
dfCarat_clarity <- dfInput %>% group_by(clarity) %>% summarise(carat = median(carat, na.rm = T))

These plots explain the strange box plots of the bivariate analysis:

  • In each carat group, the median price usually goes up as clarity gets better. The effect is clearest for the heaviest diamonds: the median price goes from $3,985 for I1 to $10,332 for IF. The prices of the best grades (VVS2 to IF) are close to each other, and they are not always in order.
  • In each group, price also goes up as color gets better from J to G. But the best grades (G to D) have about the same price. For the heaviest diamonds, D and E are even a little cheaper than G.
  • cut does not show a clear trend, even for diamonds of similar weight.

Diamonds with better grades seem cheaper overall because they are usually smaller. The median weight of an I1 diamond is 1.07 carat. The median weight of an IF diamond is only 0.35 carat. So carat is a confounder: it is related to both price and the grades, and it hides the true effect of the grades. To measure the effect of clarity or color, we must compare diamonds of similar weight.

Next, let’s check whether table and depth affect price together with color and clarity:

dfFeatures <- expand_grid(feat1 = c("depth","table"), feat2 = c("color","clarity")) %>% arrange(desc(feat2))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map2(dfFeatures$feat1, dfFeatures$feat2, 
                                   ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, .x, "price", .y, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), nrow = 2)

These plots do not show any pattern. So table and depth do not help to predict price.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

Does clarity together with cut or color tell us more about price? A heatmap answers this question. It shows a grid of tiles, one for each combination of two categories. The color of each tile shows the median price of the diamonds in that combination:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(c("cut","color"), ~ eda_plot_heatmap(dfInput, .x, "clarity", "price")), nrow = 2)

The second heatmap is more interesting. From the bottom left to the top right, the grades of color and clarity get better, and the median price usually goes down. Again, this is the opposite of what we expect, because the diamonds with the best color and clarity should be the most expensive. As we saw above, the reason is that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.

For cut and clarity, the median prices do not show a clear pattern. Each tile shows its number of diamonds. One combination (Fair cut and IF clarity) has fewer than 10 diamonds. Its tile is grey, because a median of so few diamonds is not reliable.

Summary

Here is what we found in this exploratory data analysis (EDA), which is the first study of a dataset before we build models:

  • price is right skewed. On a log scale, it has two peaks, so diamonds are popular in two different price ranges.
  • carat: about 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The spread of prices increases with weight. log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat).
  • cut is not balanced: about 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut.
  • color is not balanced: only about 5% of the diamonds have the color grade J.
  • clarity is not balanced at the two ends: only 1.5% of the diamonds have the grade I1, and only 3.3% have the grade IF.
  • price has a strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. table and depth have almost no correlation with price.
  • For diamonds of the same weight, clarity and color explain some of the differences in price. Overall, better grades seem to lower the price only because diamonds with better grades are usually smaller. cut has little effect.
save(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA, file = "diamondClean.Rda")

item.title: Building blocks of systematic investment strategies
item.description:
It is important to understand the building blocks of systematic investing strategies before learning how to build them. Here is a schematic from the book, Inside the Black Box - The Simple Truth about Quantitative Trading by Rishi Narang, that provides a good way to visualize these building blocks and how they fit together in a system.

The Black Box Revealed

The author had aptly titled it - The Black Box Revealed, since that is how most people perceive it to be from the outside. From this schematic, it is easier to understand and visualize how a system is built with a systematic approach.

Here are the components of the system:

  • Data - Encapsulates the processes of raw data collection, cleaning and preparation in tidy form to be used by the models.
  • Alpha Model - Describes the core strategy, product universe (stocks, ETFs, futures) and the rules to be implemented.
  • Risk Model - Describes position sizes or how capital/risk is allocated. This is just as much important as the alpha model itself.
  • Transaction Cost Model - Describes the transaction costs by product. These may be theoretical numbers while backtesting the strategy using historical data and later adjusted based on live execution data.
  • Portfolio Construction Model - Describes how a portfolio is constructed after putting together positions by product across one or more rules of the core strategy.
  • Execution Model - Encapsulates a live trading system. Describes the tactical implementation of the core strategy.
  • Research - Sound research forms the underpinning of all models and is driven by quantitative and statistical analysis.

The interactions shown are typical, although there could be more depending upon the implementation. More than one model could also be combined together, depending upon how the strategy is formulated. Nonetheless, for most practitioners looking to build a complete system from scratch, this is a pretty good blueprint.
